newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Kuwait MPs clash with government over oil policy.
newsitem.headline: Kuwait MPs clash with government over oil policy.

text.p: Kuwait's parliament challeneged the government again on Tuesday, demanding to review any deals with foreign firms involving domestic oil production and exploration.
"They ignore us and do not inform us of some issues in their early stages," leading MP Nasser al-Sanea told parliament.
Criticism on Tuesday focused mainly on Japan's Arabian Oil Co Ltd (AOC) which has the offshore concession within the border Neutral Zone which Kuwait shares with Saudi Arabia.
But Sanea also complained that Kuwait's Supreme Petroleum Council was due to meet on Wednesday "and we are concerned. We do not know what they will discuss."

Acting Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Sabah al- Ahmad al-Sabah, who is expected to chair the Council meeting, assured MPs that they would be consulted if any new oil deals are approved but stressed the separation between executive and legislative powers.

Political sources said MPs were also concerned the Council was planning to discuss the possibilty of upgrading existing fee-for-services technical assistance accords with global oil majors to a formula which could include production sharing.
Kuwait, which has an OPEC quota of two million barrels per day, controls about 10 percent of the world's oil reserves.

Oil Minister Isa al-Mazeedi also assured MPs, adding that the AOC deal, signed in 1958, would expire in about five years. The government had in 1995 agreed in principle to renew that contract but no contractual steps were taken.

But MPs, led by speaker Ahmad al-Saadoun, presented a new recommendation requesting the government "to inform parliament of details of its talks prior to signing deals with foreign firms involving investments of national oil resources."
The request, which was passed swiftly, also called for publicising the Neutral Zone deal and "competition" ahead of renewing it in line with the constitution.

Political sources say Tuesday's request, like three oil- related recommendations approved on Saturday, is largely a political and not a constitutional obligation as it was not made law. But some MPs argue that they have the constitutional right to approve any accords dealing with natural resources.
"The aim of the request is to make the government not even use its executive powers before consulting parliament first," Sanea earlier told Reuters of a smiliar request on Saturday.
Another request on Saturday called on Kuwait Petroleum Corp to coordinate investment policies with state Kuwait Investment Authority which runs a foreign portifolio of over $40 billion.
A third request asked KPC and its subsidiaries to notify parliament prior to concluding new deals or projects.
AOC plans to raise output by some 50,000 bpd to 350,000 bpd by 2000. Japanese interests hold the majority of AOC's stock while Kuwait and Riyadh each hold a 10 percent stake.
AOC's accord with Riyadh expires the year 2000.
Industry experts say giants like British Petroleum Plc, Chevron of the United States and France's Total SA were keen to sign technical deals to get involved in the Gulf state's oil industry.
"But this is a matter of national sovereignty. We do not want them to takeover parts of strategic (oil) operations," Sanea, head of parliament's financial committee, said earlier.
Kuwait is working to raise production capacity by about one million bpd to 3.5 million bpd early in the next century.
Kuwait, which gained independence from Britain in 1961, nationalised the industry in the 1970s, forming KPC in 1980 which has grown to become one of the world's 10 largest oil firms.
